title: QuickLift live gen setup: params, retries, and console tour
summary: Intro demo of Redwood hosted gen/chat API and Console; focused on streaming behavior, parameter tuning, retry/backoff patterns, and operational signals. Customer wants low-latency chat for in-app assistant with strict PII handling and SOC2 requirements; discussed pilot, benchmarks, and next steps for security docs and pricing.

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-09-27 16:00 UTC · 48 minutes · Recording available
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Eve (Redwood PM), Liam (Redwood SE), Jordan (QuickLift CTO), Priya (ML), Miguel (SRE), Nina (PM)

00:00 Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood Inference. We'll do a short walkthrough of the hosted generation API, show streaming behavior, talk about parameters, and then a quick tour of the Console. Samir will demo a couple of retry/backoff patterns at the end.
00:18 Jordan: Thanks, appreciate it. Quick context — we're building an in-app assistant inside QuickLift's dashboard, target latency ~200-300ms p50 for short prompts. Privacy is huge for us, SOC2 required and we use GCP with a VPC.
00:30 Alex: Great, that helps. We'll focus on low-latency streaming and idempotent retries so you can keep the UI snappy. Samir, do you want to start with the API call shape?
00:38 Samir: Sure thing. So the basic call is /v1/chat/completions — similar shape to what you expect. For streaming we return chunked deltas over an SSE stream. Important params: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, presence/penalty, and stream=true. Also we suggest a few patterns: prefix caching, short context windows for 1st-pass responses, and user-level KV cache for multi-turn flows.
01:05 Priya: When you say prefix caching, do you mean Redwood's automatic KV cache, or do we manage it?
01:11 Samir: Redwood has automatic prefix/KV caching for hosted requests — it can cache the model's key-value context to avoid re-sending long system prompts on every request. You can also manage client-side caching if you need stricter control. The console shows cache hit/miss rates.
01:28 Miguel: Any gotchas with streaming and long-running tokens? We have flaky mobile connections.
01:34 Samir: Yes, mobile churn is common. Pattern: short initial timeouts + client-side incremental backoff. We recommend idempotency-key for every user request so if the client retries, the backend deduplicates. For streaming specifically, we stream partial tokens and provide chunk sequence numbers — so clients can resume from last acknowledged chunk if you want to implement resume. Note: resume requires a consistent model version pinned.
02:05 Nina: Can you show a console trace of a streaming request?
02:09 Alex: Yeah, hopping over to the Console. (screen share) Here you can see a live request, token cost breakdown, and timing waterfall — queue time, first-byte, and per-token latency. You can filter by model, route, or token length distribution. The cost per token is surfaced per-route which helps with budget alerts.
03:12 Samir: On parameter tuning: temperature 0.0-0.2 for deterministic short answers; 0.6-0.9 for creative. For few-shot we recommend increasing max_tokens carefully — batch longer responses in background. Also top_p is a good guardrail if devs accidentally bump temperature too high.
03:40 Priya: Our assistant needs consistent replies for policy decisions — low variance is preferred.
03:43 Samir: Then stick with temperature 0.0-0.1 and deterministic sampling. Also use system instructions and few-shot examples pinned in the request, or manage them via persistent context on Redwood.
04:02 Jordan: How do retries work at your side? If we get a transient 5xx, do you auto-retry?
04:09 Samir: By default hosted API will not automatically retry on customer behalf for non-idempotent routes. We recommend client retry with exponential backoff plus jitter. For simple generate calls you should set an idempotency-key header to allow safe retries. For session/chat flows we recommend route-specific retry policies — in Console you can set a fallback to a smaller, cheaper model if the primary times out.
05:00 Miguel: Any advice on backoff times for interactive latency targets? If we want 200ms p50, long exponential backoff might break UX.
05:08 Samir: Right — short initial backoff (100-200ms) for transient rate-limit or network hiccups, then escalate. Also use local optimistic rendering — show partial streaming tokens to the user while you re-try in background.
05:30 Eve: On the security front, QuickLift asked about SOC2, SAML, and KMS. Alex, can you recap what we support?
05:38 Alex: Sure. Hosted API customers get SOC2 Type II reports on request; SAML/SSO for Console access; RBAC in console; and customer-managed keys via KMS for Private deployments. For hosted, we encrypt at rest and in transit and log audit trails. We'll send the security pack after the call.
06:01 Jordan: Data residency — can we ensure EU residency?
06:05 Alex: Yes, you can pin requests to region-specific endpoints. For stricter data residency or on-prem you can use Redwood Private. We'll include that in the options.
06:18 Priya: I want to dig into latency tradeoffs — quantization, model variants, and batching.
06:22 Samir: Short answer: lower precision (int8 quant) reduces memory and can improve throughput but may slightly affect quality. For low-latency single-turn chat, smaller model variants with optimized kernels often beat a big quantized model. Batching improves throughput but hurts single-request latency, so for interactive use we recommend very small batch sizes or request-level priority lanes (available in Dedicated). In hosted, we have smart routing that can pick a lower-cost variant if latency SLOs are met.
07:05 Priya: Can we force a model pin for the pilot?
07:07 Alex: Absolutely — you can pin a model version in your project settings. We'll pin the same version for bench runs to keep results comparable.
07:14 Samir: Now I'll run a quick sample stream. (demo) Sending a 20-token prompt, stream=true. You can see the client receives partial chunks at ~60ms intervals. The console trace shows per-token latency and a small KV cache hit.
08:01 Miguel: Looks good. Any numeric SLA on first byte or p99 token latency?
08:06 Alex: For hosted we publish typical p50/p90 numbers per model in the Model Catalog; SLA-backed latency targets are part of Dedicated contracts. We'll include typical histograms in the follow-up.
08:26 Nina: If a stream is interrupted mid-response and client retries with same idempotency key, will Redwood return the rest or replay full response?
08:34 Samir: With idempotency the server returns the same final completion; for resume semantics with chunk sequence it's possible to request only remaining chunks if you use a resume token. Otherwise the default is to re-run generation which, with pinned model and seeds, will be consistent enough for deterministic configs.
09:05 Jordan: Our workloads have peaks at end of month — bursting capacity matters. How do you handle bursty traffic?
09:11 Alex: Hosted supports autoscaling; Dedicated offers reserved capacity with burst pools you can buy. Console allows setting burst budgets and alerts when you hit thresholds. For strict capacity guarantees Dedicated is the route.
09:36 Priya: For the bench run, we want 95th latency under 600ms for typical 30-token replies.
09:41 Samir: Noted. We'll run bench with your sample traces. We'll test both a small model pinned and a quantized variant to compare cost/latency/quality.
10:03 Alex: Quick note on observability — the Console exposes token-level cost, per-route latency breakdown, and an evals tab where you can store prompt sets to detect regressions. That ties into Optimize recommendations for batching and quant profiles.
10:30 Nina: Walk me through how evals trigger alerts?
10:33 Eve: You upload a baseline prompt set, set a quality threshold (BLEU/ROUGE/custom), and the system runs periodic checks; if quality drops beyond tolerance it opens an alert and can trigger a rollback policy for rollouts.
11:00 Jordan: Okay great. Demo looks good — show us a failure/retry case?
11:06 Samir: Yep. I'll simulate a transient 503. (demo) Client retries with exponential backoff and idempotency-key set. The Console shows the error, retry counts, and then final success; also shows cost attribution per retry attempt so you can see impact on bill. Note: you can enable automatic client-side retry wrappers in our SDKs.
12:05 Priya: Does the SDK implement jittered exponential backoff by default?
12:10 Samir: Yes, our SDKs have a default policy you can tune. They also surface helpful metrics to your telemetry endpoint so you can alert on retry rate.
12:35 Jordan: About billing — does a retried request count as full tokens twice?
12:40 Alex: If you re-run generation you'll incur tokens for each attempt. If you use resume semantics or idempotency return from cache it may not double-charge. Console clarifies charge breaks by attempt. We'll review examples in the follow-up.
13:02 Miguel: Any integration with our existing observability (DataDog)?
13:06 Liam: Yes, we support pushing traces and logs to external sinks — there's a small agent/integration and webhooks. We'll share the integration guide.
13:20 Priya: A small nit — how deterministic is the model with sampling turned off? We need exact reproducibility for debugging.
13:25 Samir: With temperature 0, pinned model/version and same prompt context, generation is highly reproducible. Minor nondeterminism can appear with certain kernels, but it's rare. We can run deterministic bench tests to confirm.
14:00 Jordan: Can you summarize pilot proposals and deliverables?
14:04 Alex: Pilot: 2-week bench run — Redwood runs latency/cost tests using your sample traffic; we'll provide console access, security pack, and a small reserved capacity if needed. Deliverables: bench results, optimization recommendations, and a proposed pricing estimate.
14:30 Nina: Sounds good. Any blockers from compliance?
14:33 Alex: We'll send SOC2 and encryption docs. If you need on-prem or Private, we can scope that but it'll need a separate procurement track.
14:50 Samir: I'll add a note — for bench runs please provide a representative payload sample and expected concurrency.
15:05 Jordan: We'll share that by tomorrow.
15:12 Alex: Sweet. Final wrap: I'll send security pack, pricing, and the bench schedule. Samir will run the bench and follow up with Miguel and Priya. Any other questions?
15:26 Priya: One last — do you have any built-in token budgeting alerts?
15:30 Alex: Yes, Console supports per-route budgets with slack windows and email/pager alerts.
15:38 Jordan: Thanks everyone, that's helpful.
15:42 Alex: Thanks, we'll follow up.

End of transcript.
